title: On Having Intellectual Integrity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece defines 'intellectual integrity' as a standard that goes beyond basic honesty and transparency, describing leaders who candidly share their best current understanding of the truth while acknowledging they could be wrong. Such leaders set aside desired outcomes in favor of evidence, concede truth wherever it comes from, and are comfortable admitting when they don't know something — while remaining confident enough to act on what they do know. The essay frames self-awareness of one's own biases as central to this trait, and closes by describing intellectual integrity as a road leaders travel toward, constrained by evidence and sound argument rather than personal preference.
points: Intellectual integrity goes beyond basic honesty, openness, and transparency.
Leaders with this trait share their reasoned views candidly while acknowledging they could be wrong.
They set aside desired outcomes and rely on evidence and analysis to reach conclusions.
They are comfortable admitting when they don't know something, while remaining confident in what they do know.
Self-awareness of one's own biases and blinders is central to sustaining intellectual integrity.
quotes: Leaders are also expected to operate with an Intellectual Integrity beyond the foundational ideals of honesty, openness, and transparency.
Leaders with Intellectual Integrity candidly share their version of truth (small t, not capital T), knowing full well they could be wrong or misguided.
When making decisions, those leaders with Intellectual Integrity set aside desired outcomes and depend on factual evidence and analysis to reach conclusions.
Intellectual Integrity requires leaders to be comfortable not knowing, and they are quick to say they “don’t know” when they don’t.
The ability to see the world as it really is, and not how they wish it to be, is the hallmark of a leader with Intellectual Integrity.
